S01.question: to ask, of Scripture’s own bridal texts, to whom the Bride identity actually belongs — and to test Paul’s marriage imagery in Ephesians 5 and 2 Corinthians 11 against the assumption that a shared figure of speech transfers Israel’s prophetic identity to the Body.
S01.distinction: This is not a study of the New Covenant’s own terms, which Study 12 traces in its own right, nor of the broad Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast. Its task is narrower: to ask, of Scripture’s own bridal texts, to whom the Bride identity actually belongs — and to test Paul’s marriage imagery in Ephesians 5 and 2 Corinthians 11 against the assumption that a shared figure of speech transfers Israel’s prophetic identity to the Body.

S02.question: to define the Kingdom announcement on its own terms — audience, content, and required response — and to test that definition against Study 43’s Gospel of the Grace of God, the message most likely to be confused with it.
S02.distinction: This is not a study of Peter’s Pentecost appeal, which Study 20 reads in its own setting, nor of how Peter’s and Paul’s commissions run side by side, which Study 18 compares directly, nor of the vocabulary itself, which Study 41 settles before either message is read. Its task is narrower: to define the Kingdom announcement on its own terms — audience, content, and required response — and to test that definition against Study 43’s Gospel of the Grace of God, the message most likely to be confused with it.

S03.question: to ask which revealed program — Israel’s Prophecy or the Body’s Mystery — actually governs the coming Tribulation, and whether the Body’s own hope belongs inside that period at all.
S03.distinction: This is not a study of Daniel’s seventieth week itself, which Study 10 establishes in its own right, nor of the “one taken, one left” scene in Matthew 24 and Luke 17, which Study 29 examines on its own terms. Its task is narrower: to ask which revealed program — Israel’s Prophecy or the Body’s Mystery — actually governs the coming Tribulation, and whether the Body’s own hope belongs inside that period at all.

S04.question: Its task is broader and prior to both: to establish, from Prophecy and Mystery themselves, the controlling distinctions in origin, covenant, calling, and destiny — and to ask what a passage must actually show before any promise, covenant, or identity is carried from one program to the other.
S04.distinction: This is not a study of the threefold distinction in 1 Corinthians 10:32, which Study 36 works out on its own terms, nor of how the Church should read Israel’s own Scriptures, which Study 39 addresses directly. Its task is broader and prior to both: to establish, from Prophecy and Mystery themselves, the controlling distinctions in origin, covenant, calling, and destiny — and to ask what a passage must actually show before any promise, covenant, or identity is carried from one program to the other.
S04.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S05.question: to map the heavenly calling itself — position, citizenship, hope, conflict, and purpose — as one coherent whole, and to keep that whole calling from being reduced to any one of its own parts.
S05.distinction: This is not a study of Ephesians 2:6’s own claim that believers are seated with Christ, which Study 30 examines on its own terms, nor of the believer’s full identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys across union, standing, and conduct. Its task is narrower: to map the heavenly calling itself — position, citizenship, hope, conflict, and purpose — as one coherent whole, and to keep that whole calling from being reduced to any one of its own parts.

S06.question: to define the Mystery’s actual revealed content — the one Body, union with Christ, heavenly position — and to keep that content distinct from Prophecy without disturbing Israel’s own promises.
S06.distinction: This is not a study of when the Body of Christ began, which Study 11 asks directly, nor of Paul’s own Acts 9 calling within the continuing narrative, which Study 14 places in its setting, nor of the gospel Paul preached, which Study 43 defines on its own terms. Its task is narrower: to define the Mystery’s actual revealed content — the one Body, union with Christ, heavenly position — and to keep that content distinct from Prophecy without disturbing Israel’s own promises.

S07.question: to establish the prophetic Day of the Lord from the Prophets themselves — its judgment, darkness, and Israel’s restoration — and to keep the Body’s hope of gathering to Christ from being absorbed into a Day that belongs to a different program.
S07.distinction: This is not a study of Paul’s own Day-of-Christ expressions, which Study 8 traces on their own terms, nor of whether the Body belongs inside the coming Tribulation, which Study 3 examines directly. Its task is narrower: to establish the prophetic Day of the Lord from the Prophets themselves — its judgment, darkness, and Israel’s restoration — and to keep the Body’s hope of gathering to Christ from being absorbed into a Day that belongs to a different program.

S08.question: to define the Day of Christ strictly from Paul’s own language — gathering, resurrection, evaluation, and reward — and to keep the Judgment Seat’s review of service from being read as a judgment of sin or condemnation.
S08.distinction: This is not a study of the prophetic Day of the Lord itself, which Study 7 establishes from the Prophets, nor of Scripture’s judgments generally, which Study 31 classifies by subject, time, and standard. Its task is narrower: to define the Day of Christ strictly from Paul’s own language — gathering, resurrection, evaluation, and reward — and to keep the Judgment Seat’s review of service from being read as a judgment of sin or condemnation.

S09.question: to follow the preserved believing remnant through Elijah, Paul, and Israel’s prophetic future, and to show that a remnant’s preservation confirms Israel’s continuation rather than her replacement.
S09.distinction: This is not a study of Israel’s present corporate judicial blinding, which Study 21 examines fully, nor of Revelation’s numbered company of 144,000, which Study 23 identifies on its own terms, nor of election itself, which Study 50 traces as a distinct national and individual reality. Its task is narrower: to follow the preserved believing remnant through Elijah, Paul, and Israel’s prophetic future, and to show that a remnant’s preservation confirms Israel’s continuation rather than her replacement.

S10.question: to establish from Daniel 9 itself whose people and city the seventieth week concerns, and to show that its remaining week awaits Israel’s own future fulfillment rather than the Body’s.
S10.distinction: This is not a study of whether the Body of Christ belongs inside the coming Tribulation, which Study 3 asks directly, nor of the wider Day of the Lord that Tribulation sits within, which Study 7 traces from the Prophets. Its task is narrower: to establish from Daniel 9 itself whose people and city the seventieth week concerns, and to show that its remaining week awaits Israel’s own future fulfillment rather than the Body’s.

S11.question: to fix the Body’s actual beginning against Pentecost’s continuing Prophecy setting, and to ask what evidence — not assumption — a timing claim for the Body requires.
S11.distinction: This is not a study of the Acts 9 narrative itself, which Study 14 examines in its own right, nor of the Mystery’s full revealed content, which Study 6 identifies on its own terms, nor of the gospel that places a believer into the Body, which Study 43 defines separately. Its task is narrower: to fix the Body’s actual beginning against Pentecost’s continuing Prophecy setting, and to ask what evidence — not assumption — a timing claim for the Body requires.

S12.question: to read Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 on their own terms, and to ask whether Christ’s blood changes the covenant’s named recipients or only supplies its basis.
S12.distinction: This is not a study of how the Church may learn from Scripture written to Israel, which Study 39 works out as a general method, nor of the broad Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast. Its task is narrower: to read Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 on their own terms, and to ask whether Christ’s blood changes the covenant’s named recipients or only supplies its basis.

S13.question: to read Romans 11’s root, branches, and grafting on their own terms, and to ask what grafting actually changes — participation and standing, not national or programmatic identity.
S13.distinction: This is not a study of the Abrahamic covenant’s own terms, which Study 17 establishes in Genesis itself, nor of Paul’s several uses of Abraham’s seed, which Study 40 traces across Romans and Galatians, nor of the believing remnant within Israel, which Study 9 follows in its own right. Its task is narrower: to read Romans 11’s root, branches, and grafting on their own terms, and to ask what grafting actually changes — participation and standing, not national or programmatic identity.

S14.question: to read the Acts 9 narrative itself in its own setting, and to show that Paul’s new beginning did not require Peter’s Kingdom ministry to end.
S14.distinction: This is not a study of when the Body of Christ began as a doctrinal question, which Study 11 argues from revealed content rather than narrative alone, nor of how Peter’s and Paul’s commissions run concurrently after this point, which Study 18 compares directly. Its task is narrower: to read the Acts 9 narrative itself in its own setting, and to show that Paul’s new beginning did not require Peter’s Kingdom ministry to end.

S15.question: to read James 2 and Romans 4 each within its own stated audience, and to show that James’s covenantal, Israel-oriented setting does not contradict Paul’s exclusion of works from the ground of justification.
S15.distinction: This is not a study of Paul’s fuller Abraham argument across Romans and Galatians, which Study 40 traces on its own terms, nor of the Acts 15 dispute over circumcision and the law, which Study 19 examines as its own controversy. Its task is narrower: to read James 2 and Romans 4 each within its own stated audience, and to show that James’s covenantal, Israel-oriented setting does not contradict Paul’s exclusion of works from the ground of justification.

S16.question: Its task is broader: to survey the believer’s whole standing in Christ — union, acceptance, completeness, and security — of which each of those studies treats a single part.
S16.distinction: This is not a study of Paul’s new-creation language specifically, which Study 37 examines closely, nor of the believer’s present-tense walk by the Spirit, which Study 44 traces from Galatians 5 and Romans 8, nor of sanctification alone, which Study 45 isolates as one member of this identity. Its task is broader: to survey the believer’s whole standing in Christ — union, acceptance, completeness, and security — of which each of those studies treats a single part.
S16.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S17.question: to establish the covenant’s own terms in Genesis — line, land, nation, and blessing — before any later passage builds on them.
S17.distinction: This is not a study of Paul’s later uses of Abraham and his seed, which Study 40 traces across Romans and Galatians, nor of Romans 11’s olive-tree image built on this covenant, which Study 13 reads in its own setting, nor of how the Church learns from Genesis without acquiring its promises, which Study 39 addresses as a general method. Its task is narrower: to establish the covenant’s own terms in Genesis — line, land, nation, and blessing — before any later passage builds on them.

S18.question: to compare Peter’s and Paul’s audiences, commissions, and authority directly, and to show that recognition and fellowship between them (Galatians 2) did not require identical assignments.
S18.distinction: This is not a study of the Jerusalem Council itself, which Study 19 examines as its own dispute and decree, nor of Paul’s Acts 9 calling in its narrative setting, which Study 14 traces on its own terms. Its task is narrower: to compare Peter’s and Paul’s audiences, commissions, and authority directly, and to show that recognition and fellowship between them (Galatians 2) did not require identical assignments.

S19.question: to read Acts 15 as a concrete controversy — whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and placed under Israel’s Mosaic administration — and to show what the council actually decided, not what later disputes assume it decided.
S19.distinction: This is not a study of Peter’s and Paul’s commissions in general, which Study 18 compares on its own terms, nor of James 2’s own treatment of faith and works, which Study 15 reads within its own setting, nor of circumcision traced as a whole subject, which Study 51 examines in full. Its task is narrower: to read Acts 15 as a concrete controversy — whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and placed under Israel’s Mosaic administration — and to show what the council actually decided, not what later disputes assume it decided.

S20.question: to read Peter’s actual commands in Acts 2:38 within their own audience and prophetic setting, and to show what he promised, to whom, and on what ground.
S20.distinction: This is not a study of the Kingdom message Peter’s hearers had already heard, which Study 2 defines on its own terms, nor of the apostles’ later renewed Spirit filling in Acts 4, which Study 34 distinguishes from Pentecost, nor of the general test for whether an Acts narrative obligates the Body today, which Study 38 supplies. Its task is narrower: to read Peter’s actual commands in Acts 2:38 within their own audience and prophetic setting, and to show what he promised, to whom, and on what ground.

S21.question: to fix the exact extent of Israel’s corporate hardening — what it covers and what it leaves untouched — and to ask whether a judicial suspension of Israel’s national administration can ever be read as canceling a covenant promise rather than merely postponing its exercise.
S21.distinction: This is not a study of the believing remnant’s own continued existence within Israel, which Study 9 follows in its own right, nor of Romans 11’s olive-tree image of branches broken off and grafted in, which Study 13 reads on its own terms. Its task is narrower: to fix the exact extent of Israel’s corporate hardening — what it covers and what it leaves untouched — and to ask whether a judicial suspension of Israel’s national administration can ever be read as canceling a covenant promise rather than merely postponing its exercise.

S22.question: to read the Kingdom’s own prayer promises in their original setting, and to build the Body’s actual practice of prayer from what Paul himself reveals — not from a Kingdom-era promise transferred without its terms.
S22.distinction: This is not a study of the believer’s whole standing in Christ, which Study 16 surveys in full, nor of the general method for learning from Scripture addressed to Israel, which Study 39 supplies, nor of another practice reframed under grace, which Study 47 traces for giving. Its task is narrower: to read the Kingdom’s own prayer promises in their original setting, and to build the Body’s actual practice of prayer from what Paul himself reveals — not from a Kingdom-era promise transferred without its terms.

S23.question: to ask what a specific, numbered, sealed company can be shown to be from the text alone, and to keep that one company from absorbing every promise Scripture makes to a faithful Israelite.
S23.distinction: This is not a study of Israel’s believing remnant generally, which Study 9 follows across her whole history, nor of Revelation’s seven churches and their own setting, which Study 26 examines first. Its task is narrower: to ask what a specific, numbered, sealed company can be shown to be from the text alone, and to keep that one company from absorbing every promise Scripture makes to a faithful Israelite.

S24.question: to trace Hebrews 10:26’s own argument, audience, and covenant setting, and to show why its warning belongs to that setting rather than to Paul’s teaching for the Body of Christ.
S24.distinction: This is not a study of Hebrews 6’s earlier warning and its land illustration, which Study 28 examines on its own terms, nor of the New Covenant promise whose recipients give Hebrews its covenant weight, which Study 12 establishes separately. Its task is narrower: to trace Hebrews 10:26’s own argument, audience, and covenant setting, and to show why its warning belongs to that setting rather than to Paul’s teaching for the Body of Christ.

S25.question: to read Mark 16:20 on its own terms — signs confirming the word preached by commissioned messengers — and to keep that stated purpose from becoming a checklist for every believer.
S25.distinction: This is not a study of the general test for moving from an Acts-era event to a present obligation, which Study 38 supplies, nor of the apostles’ repeated Spirit filling, which Study 34 distinguishes from a sign’s confirming purpose, nor of the baptisms Scripture actually describes, which Study 42 classifies in full. Its task is narrower: to read Mark 16:20 on its own terms — signs confirming the word preached by commissioned messengers — and to keep that stated purpose from becoming a checklist for every believer.

S26.question: to ask what the word church actually requires of an assembly named in Revelation 2–3, and to keep that word from settling, by itself, whether any one of the seven is the Church which is Christ’s Body.
S26.distinction: This is not a study of the separately identified 144,000 later in Revelation, which Study 23 examines on its own terms, nor of Daniel’s own prophetic timetable, which Study 10 establishes first. Its task is narrower: to ask what the word church actually requires of an assembly named in Revelation 2–3, and to keep that word from settling, by itself, whether any one of the seven is the Church which is Christ’s Body.

S27.question: to read Leviticus 23’s feasts in their own setting of land, harvest, and priestly service, and to ask which of Christ’s own fulfillments are already accomplished and which remain tied to Israel’s still-future calendar.
S27.distinction: This is not a study of the general method for learning from Israel’s commands without taking over her covenant obligations, which Study 39 supplies, nor of the New Covenant’s own named recipients, which Study 12 establishes separately. Its task is narrower: to read Leviticus 23’s feasts in their own setting of land, harvest, and priestly service, and to ask which of Christ’s own fulfillments are already accomplished and which remain tied to Israel’s still-future calendar.

S28.question: to read every description in Hebrews 6:4–6 in its own argument and audience, and to ask what the land illustration and the “better things” that follow actually settle about the warning’s force.
S28.distinction: This is not a study of Hebrews 10’s distinct warning about repudiating the Son, which Study 24 traces on its own terms, nor of Scripture’s judgments generally, which Study 31 classifies by subject and standard, nor of the Body’s security under grace, which Study 46 establishes from a different covenant altogether. Its task is narrower: to read every description in Hebrews 6:4–6 in its own argument and audience, and to ask what the land illustration and the “better things” that follow actually settle about the warning’s force.

S29.question: to read Matthew 24 and Luke 17 on their own terms, and to show that being “taken” in this scene means judgment overtaking the unprepared, not the Body’s gathering to Christ.
S29.distinction: This is not a study of whether the Body belongs in Israel’s coming Tribulation, which Study 3 asks directly, nor of the wider Day-of-the-Lord judgment the Tribulation sits within, which Study 7 traces from the Prophets, nor of the Body’s own heavenly resurrection, which Study 49 distinguishes from every other resurrection Scripture names. Its task is narrower: to read Matthew 24 and Luke 17 on their own terms, and to show that being “taken” in this scene means judgment overtaking the unprepared, not the Body’s gathering to Christ.

S30.question: to test Ephesians 2:6’s specific claim — that believers are seated with Christ — against the further, more ambitious claims sometimes built on it, and to keep what the text actually establishes distinct from what is merely inferred.
S30.distinction: This is not a study of the Body’s whole heavenly calling, which Study 5 maps across position, citizenship, hope, and purpose, nor of the believer’s full identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys across union, standing, and conduct. Its task is narrower: to test Ephesians 2:6’s specific claim — that believers are seated with Christ — against the further, more ambitious claims sometimes built on it, and to keep what the text actually establishes distinct from what is merely inferred.

S31.question: Its task is broader: to classify every major judgment complex in Scripture by subject, time, standard, and outcome, so that no two of them are collapsed into a single undifferentiated “judgment.”
S31.distinction: This is not a study of crowns and rewards in their own passages, which Study 33 examines directly, nor of Paul’s own Day-of-Christ language, which Study 8 defines on its own terms, nor of the believer’s security under grace, which Study 46 argues from a different set of texts. Its task is broader: to classify every major judgment complex in Scripture by subject, time, standard, and outcome, so that no two of them are collapsed into a single undifferentiated “judgment.”
S31.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S32.question: Its task is broader and prior to both: to compare the two organizing frameworks themselves — how each connects promise to fulfillment and assigns covenant recipients — and to test their genuine differences against Scripture rather than against each other’s caricatures.
S32.distinction: This is not a study of the Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes on its own terms, nor of the specific method for learning from Israel’s Scriptures, which Study 39 supplies as a working rule. Its task is broader and prior to both: to compare the two organizing frameworks themselves — how each connects promise to fulfillment and assigns covenant recipients — and to test their genuine differences against Scripture rather than against each other’s caricatures.
S32.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S33.question: to ask, of each individual crown passage, who receives it, for what, and under what image — service, endurance, shepherding, or royal supremacy — so that one familiar word never flattens several distinct pictures into a single reward.
S33.distinction: This is not a study of Scripture’s judgments as a whole, which Study 31 classifies by subject, time, and standard, nor of Paul’s own Day-of-Christ language, which Study 8 defines on its own terms. Its task is narrower: to ask, of each individual crown passage, who receives it, for what, and under what image — service, endurance, shepherding, or royal supremacy — so that one familiar word never flattens several distinct pictures into a single reward.

S34.question: to show, from Acts 2 and Acts 4 themselves, that a second filling of the same praying company renews enablement for an immediate assignment rather than repeating salvation or indwelling.
S34.distinction: This is not a study of Peter’s original Pentecost promise, which Study 20 reads in its own audience and setting, nor of the general test for whether an Acts event obligates the Body today, which Study 38 supplies, nor of the Body’s own settled indwelling by the Spirit, which Study 44 distinguishes from any repeated filling. Its task is narrower: to show, from Acts 2 and Acts 4 themselves, that a second filling of the same praying company renews enablement for an immediate assignment rather than repeating salvation or indwelling.

S35.question: to test each disputed identity expression — Galatians 6:16, Romans 2:28–29, “spiritual Israel” — within its own passage, rather than letting one debated phrase govern how the others are read.
S35.distinction: This is not a study of the broad Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast, nor of Paul’s threefold categories in 1 Corinthians 10:32, which Study 36 works out on its own terms, nor of Paul’s uses of Abraham’s seed, which Study 40 traces across Romans and Galatians. Its task is narrower: to test each disputed identity expression — Galatians 6:16, Romans 2:28–29, “spiritual Israel” — within its own passage, rather than letting one debated phrase govern how the others are read.

S36.question: to fix 1 Corinthians 10:32’s three named categories to Paul’s own case — a Jew by descent who stands in the Body as a member of it, not as Israel — and to show that a single verse naming three groups was never meant to erase what distinguishes them.
S36.distinction: This is not a study of the broad Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast, nor of the disputed identity expressions tested in Study 35, such as “Israel of God” and “spiritual Israel.” Its task is narrower: to fix 1 Corinthians 10:32’s three named categories to Paul’s own case — a Jew by descent who stands in the Body as a member of it, not as Israel — and to show that a single verse naming three groups was never meant to erase what distinguishes them.

S37.question: to test what “new creation” itself asserts — an accomplished standing, not gradual moral improvement — and to keep that accomplished fact distinct from Israel’s own future national renewal.
S37.distinction: This is not a study of the believer’s whole identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys broadly, nor of the Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast, nor of the believer’s present-tense walk by the Spirit, which Study 44 examines from Galatians 5 and Romans 8. Its task is narrower: to test what “new creation” itself asserts — an accomplished standing, not gradual moral improvement — and to keep that accomplished fact distinct from Israel’s own future national renewal.

S38.question: Its task is broader: to supply the actual test for deciding when any Acts-era event creates a present obligation for the Body, a test each of those studies then applies to its own passage.
S38.distinction: This is not a study of Peter’s Pentecost commands themselves, which Study 20 reads in their own audience, nor of Mark 16’s sign commission, which Study 25 examines on its own terms, nor of the apostles’ renewed Spirit filling, which Study 34 distinguishes from Pentecost. Its task is broader: to supply the actual test for deciding when any Acts-era event creates a present obligation for the Body, a test each of those studies then applies to its own passage.
S38.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S39.question: Its task is broader: to supply the repeatable method itself — preserving what God said, to whom, and in what setting — that each of those studies applies to its own passage.
S39.distinction: This is not a study of the Abrahamic covenant’s own terms, which Study 17 establishes in Genesis, nor of Paul’s specific uses of Abraham’s history, which Study 40 traces as a worked example, nor of the parallel question for Acts narratives, which Study 38 answers on its own terms. Its task is broader: to supply the repeatable method itself — preserving what God said, to whom, and in what setting — that each of those studies applies to its own passage.
S39.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S40.question: to follow Paul’s own uses of Abraham’s seed passage by passage, and to show that the phrase names different groups in different arguments rather than one sweeping identity.
S40.distinction: This is not a study of the Abrahamic covenant’s own original terms, which Study 17 establishes in Genesis, nor of Romans 11’s olive-tree image built on that covenant, which Study 13 reads in its own setting, nor of the general method for learning from Israel’s Scriptures, which Study 39 supplies. Its task is narrower: to follow Paul’s own uses of Abraham’s seed passage by passage, and to show that the phrase names different groups in different arguments rather than one sweeping identity.

S41.question: Its task comes first: to settle, from the Gospels themselves, whether “kingdom of heaven” and “kingdom of God” name one kingdom or two before either later study is read.
S41.distinction: This is not a study of what Israel was called to do in response to the Kingdom, which Study 2 examines in full, nor of the Body’s own heavenly calling, which Study 5 develops as a whole, nor of the Acts 28 suspension of Israel’s program, which Study 21 traces directly. Its task comes first: to settle, from the Gospels themselves, whether “kingdom of heaven” and “kingdom of God” name one kingdom or two before either later study is read.
S41.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S42.question: Its task is broader: to classify every baptism Scripture names — by agent, element, and result — and to identify which one alone places a believer into the Body.
S42.distinction: This is not a study of Peter’s Pentecost command in isolation, which Study 20 reads in its own audience and setting, nor of Mark 16’s sign commission joining belief and baptism, which Study 25 examines on its own terms, nor of the Spirit’s repeated fillings in Acts, which Study 34 distinguishes from a once-for-all baptism. Its task is broader: to classify every baptism Scripture names — by agent, element, and result — and to identify which one alone places a believer into the Body.
S42.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S43.question: to hold Paul’s gospel to his own stated terms rather than a general definition of the word, and to show why treating it as one more variation on a message announced to Israel empties his own distinctions of their force.
S43.distinction: This is not a study of the Kingdom message Israel was called to believe, which Study 2 defines on its own terms, nor of the Mystery’s full revealed content, which Study 6 identifies separately, nor of when the Body itself began, which Study 11 asks directly. Its task is narrower: to hold Paul’s gospel to his own stated terms rather than a general definition of the word, and to show why treating it as one more variation on a message announced to Israel empties his own distinctions of their force.

S44.question: It assumes each of those and asks a different question: given who the believer already is, how is the believer meant to walk, day by day?
S44.distinction: This study is not a study of the believer's identity in Christ, which Study 16 examines, nor of the Acts-era fillings of the Spirit, which Study 34 examines, nor of the believer's new-creation standing, which Study 37 examines. It assumes each of those and asks a different question: given who the believer already is, how is the believer meant to walk, day by day?
S44.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S45.question: how many distinct things is Paul actually saying when he uses sanctification language, and how does each relate to Israel's holiness under the Law?
S45.distinction: This study is not a study of the believer's whole identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys broadly, nor of the moment-by-moment conflict between the flesh and the Spirit, which Study 44 examines from Galatians 5 and Romans 8, nor of the believer's new-creation standing, which Study 37 examines on its own terms. It assumes each of those and asks a narrower question: how many distinct things is Paul actually saying when he uses sanctification language, and how does each relate to Israel's holiness under the Law?

S46.question: once a standing is given in Christ, is that standing ever revocable?
S46.distinction: This study is not a general study of the believer’s identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys broadly, nor a re-argument of Hebrews 6:4–6, which Study 28 examines on its own terms, nor a full classification of biblical judgments, which Study 31 undertakes. It assumes each of those and asks a narrower question: once a standing is given in Christ, is that standing ever revocable?

S47.question: once grace, not law, is the ground of giving, what does Paul actually require, and what does he leave to the giver?
S47.distinction: This study is not a general study of the believer's identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys broadly, nor a full treatment of prayer under grace, which Study 22 examines in its own right, nor a comparison of covenant frameworks, which Study 32 undertakes. It asks a narrower question: once grace, not law, is the ground of giving, what does Paul actually require, and what does he leave to the giver?

S48.question: once every household relationship flows from grace rather than law, what does Paul actually require of each party, and where does that authority answer?
S48.distinction: This is not a general study of the believer's identity in Christ, which Study 16 surveys broadly, nor a study of sanctification under grace, which Study 45 examines in its own right, nor a study of giving, which Study 47 traces from 2 Corinthians. It asks a narrower question: once every household relationship flows from grace rather than law, what does Paul actually require of each party, and where does that authority answer?

S49.question: when Scripture uses the word "resurrection," how many distinct events does it actually name, and what governs which one applies to whom?
S49.distinction: This is not a general study of the Body's future hope, which Study 8 examines through Paul's Day-of-Christ language, nor of the Great White Throne judgment itself, which Study 31 treats at length, nor of the "one taken, one left" passages in Matthew 24 and Luke 17, which Study 29 traces in their own setting. It asks a narrower question: when Scripture uses the word "resurrection," how many distinct events does it actually name, and what governs which one applies to whom?

S50.question: to ask, of every election passage in view, who is the object of the choice, on what basis, at what point, and unto what end — and to test that method against the one passage most likely to blur the two elections together, 1 Peter 1:1–2.
S50.distinction: This is not a general study of Israel's remnant, which Study 9 traces in its own right, nor of the judicial suspension that presently governs Israel's corporate unbelief, which Study 21 examines fully, nor of the broad Israel–Body distinction itself, which Study 4 establishes across every point of contrast. Its task is narrower: to ask, of every election passage in view, who is the object of the choice, on what basis, at what point, and unto what end — and to test that method against the one passage most likely to blur the two elections together, 1 Peter 1:1–2.

S51.question: to trace circumcision specifically — as a sign, as history, and as a New Testament reality — and to test that reading against the passage most likely to blur the two together, Romans 2:28–29’s “circumcision . . . of the heart.”
S51.distinction: This is not a full study of the Jerusalem Council itself, which Study 19 examines in full, nor of the Body’s one baptism, which Study 42 traces at length and which Colossians 2:11–13 pairs directly with the circumcision of Christ, nor of the Abrahamic covenant broadly, which Study 17 establishes in its own right. Its task is narrower: to trace circumcision specifically — as a sign, as history, and as a New Testament reality — and to test that reading against the passage most likely to blur the two together, Romans 2:28–29’s “circumcision . . . of the heart.”

S52.question: when Scripture applies the single word “adoption” to both Israel and the Body, what company, what ground, and what timing does each occurrence actually name?
S52.distinction: Readers who have studied Study 50 (Election) may wonder whether adoption simply restates election under another name. It does not: election concerns God's own antecedent choosing of a people or a person, while adoption names the legal placing into sonship that choice results in — a distinct link in the same chain Ephesians 1:4–5 itself states in order, “chosen . . . predestinated . . . unto the adoption.” Readers who have studied Study 44 (Walking in the Spirit) may likewise wonder whether “the Spirit of adoption” (Romans 8:15) is the same subject as the believer's Spirit-enabled walk; Study 44 traces the Spirit's present-tense ministry of enabling conduct against the flesh, while this study traces the Spirit's own witness confirming a settled legal standing already received (Romans 8:15–16) — a testimony to identity, not a summons to obedience. This study alone answers one narrower question: when Scripture applies the single word “adoption” to both Israel and the Body, what company, what ground, and what timing does each occurrence actually name?

S53.question: when Scripture applies the single word “redemption” to Israel's historical and future national deliverance and to the Body's own standing in Christ, what company, what price, and what timing does each occurrence actually name?
S53.distinction: Readers who have studied Study 52 (Sonship and Adoption) may wonder whether redemption and adoption trace the same ground, since Galatians 4:4–5 names redemption as adoption's own stated basis in a single sentence. This study examines redemption itself as the described act — the bondage answered and the price paid; Study 52 examines the legal placing into sonship that this same redemption secures, the same verse answering two different questions, not the same question answered twice. Readers who have studied Study 46 (Secure in Christ) may likewise wonder whether this study's own reference to the Spirit's seal and earnest (Ephesians 1:13–14) duplicates that study's subject; Study 46 argues from that seal and earnest for the believer's settled security against the Hebrews 6:4–6 warning, while this study reads the same verse only for what it says about redemption's own two-stage shape — a price already paid, and a possession not yet fully claimed. This study alone answers one narrower question: when Scripture applies the single word “redemption” to Israel's historical and future national deliverance and to the Body's own standing in Christ, what company, what price, and what timing does each occurrence actually name?

S54.question: when Israel's own pursuit of a law-righteousness stumbled, what did that stumbling actually prove about the law, and what did it leave untouched about righteousness by faith, as counted to Abraham?
S54.distinction: Readers who have studied Study 53 (Redemption) may wonder whether this study restates that one, since both draw on Romans 3:24 in a single verse; Study 53 traces the price redemption itself names — the bondage answered and the cost paid — while this study reads the same verse only for the verdict that price makes possible, not the price itself. Readers who have studied Study 15 (Faith and Works in James and Paul) may likewise wonder whether this study duplicates that comparison, since both touch Abraham's justification; Study 15 reads James 2 and Romans 4 each within its own stated audience to show a living faith is not a barren claim, while this study reads Romans 4 and Genesis 15:6 only for what they establish about justification's own timing and ground, not for James's distinct question. Readers of Study 40 (Who Is Abraham's Seed?) may wonder whether this study's own use of Abraham repeats that one; Study 40 traces what the word “seed” names across Paul's arguments in Romans and Galatians, while this study uses Abraham only for what Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4 state about belief counted for righteousness, not to settle who his seed are. This study alone answers one narrower question: when Israel's own pursuit of a law-righteousness stumbled, what did that stumbling actually prove about the law, and what did it leave untouched about righteousness by faith, as counted to Abraham?

S55.question: how does God’s action in Christ establish peace, and how does Paul’s appeal relate to that accomplished work?
S55.distinction: Readers who have studied Study 53 (Redemption) may wonder whether this study repeats its treatment of Christ’s blood, since both examine benefits secured through his death. Study 53 asks what bondage redemption answers and what price secures deliverance; Study 55 asks what becomes of former enemies in relation to God and why Paul announces an appeal to be reconciled. Readers of Study 54 (Justification) will encounter Romans 5:1 in both studies. Study 54 establishes the righteous verdict received by faith; this study follows the peace named in that verse and the received reconciliation of Romans 5:10–11. Study 37 (What Does Paul Mean by “New Creation”?) examines 2 Corinthians 5:17; this study follows verses 18–21 to distinguish God’s reconciling work, the entrusted message, and the hearer’s response. Study 52 (Sonship and Adoption) addresses standing and inheritance, while this study addresses enmity and peace. The question this study alone follows through all four principal passages is: how does God’s action in Christ establish peace, and how does Paul’s appeal relate to that accomplished work?

S56.question: who inherits what, on what basis, and when?
S56.distinction: Study 5 surveys the Body’s wider heavenly calling; this study examines the narrower question of what inheritance passages say an heir receives. Study 17 establishes the Abrahamic covenant’s line, land, nation, and blessing, while Study 56 follows how the promised land is held, historically possessed, and expected after dispersion. Study 40 asks how Paul uses Abraham’s seed, faith, and promise; this study compares that heir language with other apostolic inheritance passages. Study 52 establishes sonship and adoption; this study asks what follows from the status of heir. The question Study 56 alone follows across these settings is: who inherits what, on what basis, and when?

S57.question: It does not turn the Church’s witness into an unstated commission over heavenly powers or transfer Israel’s covenants to the Body.
S57.distinction: Study 6 explains the content and timing of the Mystery’s revelation. Study 5 surveys the Body’s heavenly calling, Study 30 examines its present seating with Christ, and Study 56 asks what inheritance passages grant. Study 57 joins these questions around Ephesians 3:10–11: why does the revealed Body now display God’s wisdom, and how does that present witness accord with His eternal purpose? It does not turn the Church’s witness into an unstated commission over heavenly powers or transfer Israel’s covenants to the Body.
S57.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S58.question: It also shows why Paul’s new stewardship during Acts 9–28 does not itself end Israel’s concurrent prophetic commission or cancel earlier promises.
S58.distinction: Study 6 identifies the Mystery’s content; Study 32 compares organizing theological systems; Study 57 examines eternal purpose and Christ’s headship. Study 58 supplies the narrower word and passage study needed before using “dispensation” as a system label. It also shows why Paul’s new stewardship during Acts 9–28 does not itself end Israel’s concurrent prophetic commission or cancel earlier promises.
S58.source: page (closing sentence of the distinction paragraph)

S59.question: Study 59 asks the narrower question of a command’s covenant authority.
S59.distinction: Study 4 establishes the broader Israel–Body distinction, while Study 36 explains Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God in 1 Corinthians 10:32. Study 59 asks the narrower question of a command’s covenant authority. It supplies the governing test for the circumcision, sanctification, and giving issues treated fully in Studies 19, 45, 47, and 51.

S60.question: Study 60 asks the narrower question of how a particular occurrence of church should be identified in context; it also complements Study 38’s control on narrated events and leaves the seven churches of Revelation to Study 26.
S60.distinction: Study 4 establishes Israel’s and the Body’s distinct corporate identities. Study 36 examines the threefold designation in 1 Corinthians 10:32. Study 60 asks the narrower question of how a particular occurrence of church should be identified in context; it also complements Study 38’s control on narrated events and leaves the seven churches of Revelation to Study 26.

S61.question: who are the woman, the male child, the dragon, and her offspring in Revelation 12, and what does the chapter itself establish about each of them?
S61.distinction: Readers who already own Study 9 (The Remnant), Study 23 (The 144,000), Study 7 (The Day of the Lord), or Study 10 (Daniel’s Seventieth Week) will recognize adjoining ground here. Study 9 traces the believing remnant’s preservation across Israel’s history in general terms; this study narrates one specific scene of that preservation — the woman’s flight and the dragon’s pursuit — and supplies the remnant’s Revelation 12:17 description in its own setting. Study 23 identifies the 144,000 as a numbered, sealed company within the remnant; this study extends that identification to the male child of 12:5, and treats “the rest of her offspring” in 12:17 as the wider remnant population the 144,000 belong to, not as another name for the same company. Study 7 traces the Day of the Lord’s judgment and Israel’s restoration across the prophets broadly; this study supplies one chapter’s contribution to that same period without re-deriving the whole Day-of-the-Lord chronology. Study 10 reads Daniel’s seventieth week as a seven-year unit divided at its midpoint; this study reads Revelation 12’s 1,260 days and “time, times, and half a time” as that same three-and-a-half-year half-week from the perspective of the woman rather than Daniel’s own vantage point. The question this study alone answers: who are the woman, the male child, the dragon, and her offspring in Revelation 12, and what does the chapter itself establish about each of them?

S62.question: what does Matthew 5:17–20 itself assert, of what, and to whom — and how can it and Paul’s statements about the Law each be read on its own terms?
S62.distinction: Readers who already own Study 59 (The Law’s Jurisdiction and the Body of Christ), Study 2 (The Gospel of the Kingdom), or Study 41 (Kingdom of God or Kingdom of Heaven?) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 59 traces to whom the Mosaic Law was given and on what basis Paul instructs the Body; this study does not re-derive that survey, but works one Gospel passage closely and asks how its wording sits beside Paul’s. Study 2 establishes Israel, the kingdom message, and the commission it carried; this study relies on that setting only as far as Matthew 4:17–5:2 shows it and does not rebuild the doctrine. Study 41 examines the two kingdom phrases and the distinctions Scripture draws between them; this study meets “the kingdom of heaven” in verses 19–20 but leaves the relation of the phrases to Study 41. The question this study alone answers: what does Matthew 5:17–20 itself assert, of what, and to whom — and how can it and Paul’s statements about the Law each be read on its own terms?

S63.question: what did the sign of Isaiah 7:13–16 mean to the house of David, and how does Matthew 1:22–23 say it was fulfilled?
S63.distinction: Readers who already own Study 62 (Matthew 5:17–20), Study 21 (Israel’s Judicial Blinding), or Study 9 (The Remnant) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 62 traces how Matthew uses the verb “fulfil” and lists Matthew 1:22–23 among its examples; this study does not repeat that survey, but examines the Isaiah passage that Matthew quotes. Study 21 follows the hardening announced in Isaiah 6, the chapter just before this one; this study begins at the sign that follows and does not re-derive the hardening. Study 9 traces the believing remnant across Israel’s history, and Shear-jashub’s name in Isaiah 7:3 belongs to that theme; this study meets him only as context for the scene. The question this study alone answers: what did the sign of Isaiah 7:13–16 mean to the house of David, and how does Matthew 1:22–23 say it was fulfilled?

S64.question: what does Revelation 19:6–10 announce, who is wed, and who is called to the supper?
S64.distinction: Readers who already own Study 1 (The Bride of Christ), Study 27 (Israel’s Seven Appointed Feasts), or Study 4 (Israel and the Body of Christ) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 1 traces the bridal theme through Israel’s Scriptures and tests Paul’s marriage imagery in Ephesians 5 and 2 Corinthians 11; this study takes the Bride’s identity as established there and does not argue it again. Study 27 works through the seven appointed feasts of Leviticus 23 and does not treat the marriage supper. Study 4 sets out the broad comparison of Israel and the Body, which this study assumes rather than rebuilds. The parables The Wedding Banquet and The Great Banquet narrate refused invitations to a feast in story form; this study cites them as parallel banquet images and does not teach them. The question this study alone answers: what does Revelation 19:6–10 announce, who is wed, and who is called to the supper?

S65.question: what was “the apostles’ doctrine” of Acts 2:42, and to whom did it belong?
S65.distinction: Readers who already own Study 20 (Understanding Acts 2:38), Study 38 (Why Acts Is Not a Universal Experience Manual), or Study 18 (Peter and Paul: Distinct Apostolic Commissions) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 20 interprets Peter’s appeal and the baptism he commanded; this study begins after that appeal, with what the converts did next. Study 38 sets out the method for deciding when an Acts event becomes a rule; this study applies a method of that kind to a single verse and does not re-derive it. Study 18 compares the two commissions across the whole book; this study asks the narrower question of what the Twelve’s teaching consisted of. The question this study alone answers: what was “the apostles’ doctrine” of Acts 2:42, and to whom did it belong?

S66.question: what did Jesus assign to the Eleven in Matthew 28:18–20, by what wording, and to whom?
S66.distinction: Readers who already own Study 18 (Peter and Paul: Distinct Apostolic Commissions), Study 65 (Acts 2:42), or Study 42 (One Baptism) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 18 compares the two apostolic assignments side by side; this study reads the wording of the Eleven’s commission itself and comes to Paul only in its seventh section. Study 65 asks what the Twelve taught at Jerusalem and to whom it belonged; this study stays in Galilee and asks what they were told to do. Study 42 classifies every water baptism in Acts and follows Paul’s letters to the one baptism of the Body; this study treats “baptizing” only as one word of the commission and does not re-run that classification. The question this study alone answers: what did Jesus assign to the Eleven in Matthew 28:18–20, by what wording, and to whom?

S67.question: who is Melchizedek in the three passages that name him, what does Hebrews make of his priesthood, and to whom does that argument speak?
S67.distinction: Readers who already own Study 28 (The Warning of Hebrews 6:4–6), Study 17 (The Abrahamic Covenant), or Study 12 (The New Covenant) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 28 reads the warning of Hebrews 6 in its argument; this study touches Hebrews 6 only where the oath and the forerunner (6:13–20) lead to Melchizedek. Study 17 establishes the covenant promises made to Abraham; this study treats Genesis 14 only for what it says about the king of Salem. Study 12 examines Israel’s promised restoration under Messiah; this study notes the change of priesthood and law in Hebrews 7 without re-deriving the covenant. The question this study alone answers: who is Melchizedek in the three passages that name him, what does Hebrews make of his priesthood, and to whom does that argument speak?

S68.question: what does each passage that speaks of a book of names say about it, whose names does it record, and what do the texts state about removal?
S68.distinction: Readers who already own Study 31 (The Judgments of Scripture), Study 49 (The Resurrections of Scripture), or Study 46 (Secure in Christ) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 31 classifies the judgments by subject, time, standard, and outcome; this study touches the Great White Throne only for the books and the Book of Life that Revelation 20 names. Study 49 traces the distinct resurrections, including the resurrection of the unjust; this study takes that resurrection as given and does not re-derive it. Study 46 argues the Body’s security from the seal, the earnest, and Romans 8; this study reads Revelation 3:5 in its own setting and does not re-argue that security. The question this study alone answers: what does each passage that speaks of a book of names say about it, whose names does it record, and what do the texts state about removal?

S69.question: where does Scripture place Israel and the Body in the eternal state, what do the passages state about each realm, and how are the two joined under Christ?
S69.distinction: Readers who already own Study 5 (The Heavenly Calling), Study 57 (The Eternal Purpose of God), or Study 1 (The Bride of Christ) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 5 maps the Body’s whole heavenly calling, including blessings, citizenship, and purpose; this study takes the heavenly setting as one of two realms and does not re-derive the calling. Study 57 traces God’s purpose before the ages and its future fullness; this study reads Ephesians 1:10 only for the two realms it names. Study 1 establishes to whom the bridal identity belongs; this study notes that the city of Revelation 21 is called a bride and defers the question of the identity. The question this study alone answers: where does Scripture place Israel and the Body in the eternal state, what do the passages state about each realm, and how are the two joined under Christ?

S70.question: what did Jesus mean Nicodemus to understand by “born of water and of the Spirit”?
S70.distinction: Readers who already own Study 42 (One Baptism), Study 20 (Understanding Acts 2:38), Study 37 (What Does Paul Mean by “New Creation”?), or Study 41 (Kingdom of God or Kingdom of Heaven?) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 42 classifies the baptisms recorded in Acts and follows Paul to the one baptism of the Body; this study does not classify baptisms and stays in John 3. Study 20 reads Peter’s appeal at Pentecost; John 3 was spoken before the cross and before that day. Study 37 follows a Pauline phrase; this study stays with the words Jesus spoke to Nicodemus. Study 41 compares the two kingdom phrases across the Gospels; this study asks only what “see” and “enter” mean in John 3:3, 5. The question this study alone answers: what did Jesus mean Nicodemus to understand by “born of water and of the Spirit”?

S71.question: what does each genealogy of Jesus claim for him, and why must Israel’s Messiah come through that descent?
S71.distinction: Readers who already own Study 63 (Isaiah 7:13–16), Study 17 (The Abrahamic Covenant), or Study 12 (The New Covenant) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 63 reads Isaiah’s sign to Ahaz’s house and how Matthew uses it; this study reads Matthew’s and Luke’s lists and does not take up that sign. Study 17 follows the covenant with Abraham across Scripture; this study takes only the words of descent in the promises, as they bear on a register. Study 12 reads the New Covenant; this study shares a prophet with it but reads only Jeremiah 22:24–30 and does not enter the covenant of Jeremiah 31. The question this study alone answers: what does each genealogy of Jesus claim for him, and why must Israel’s Messiah come through that descent?

S72.question: what do the passages say the Supper is, and what does the Body do when it takes the cup?
S72.distinction: Readers who already own Study 12 (The New Covenant), Study 65 (Acts 2:42: The Apostles’ Doctrine), or Study 53 (Redemption) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 12 reads the New Covenant as a covenant; this study reads only the cup’s wording and the covenant text it points to, and does not take up the covenant’s full content. Study 65 reads Acts 2:42 as a whole and asks what the Twelve’s doctrine was; this study notes the breaking of bread there only as a recorded fact and does not take up the doctrine. Study 53 follows redemption across Scripture; this study reads the blood only as the cup names it. The question this study alone answers: what do the passages say the Supper is, and what does the Body do when it takes the cup?

S73.question: what do the passages say God promised David, and to whom?
S73.distinction: Readers who already own Study 17 (The Abrahamic Covenant), Study 12 (The New Covenant), or Study 71 (The Genealogies of Jesus) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 17 follows God’s promises to Abraham; this study touches Abraham only where 2 Samuel 7 echoes that promise, and does not take up the land and seed promises. Study 12 reads the New Covenant as a covenant; this study reads only the Davidic content, including the echo in Jeremiah 33, and does not enter Jeremiah 31. Study 71 reads the two genealogies as records; this study does not handle the lists of names. The question this study alone answers: what do the passages say God promised David, and to whom?

S74.question: what does each passage say about a final ruler, an abomination, or an antichrist, and what does it leave unsaid?
S74.distinction: Readers who already own Study 10 (Daniel’s Seventieth Week), Study 7 (The Day of the Lord), or Study 61 (Revelation 12) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 10 reads Daniel’s seventieth week in relation to Daniel’s people, city, and timetable; this study reads Daniel only for the features of the rulers it names and does not take up the week’s timetable. Study 7 traces the Day of the Lord through judgment and restoration; this study reads the one paragraph of 2 Thessalonians 2 and does not settle the day’s wording. Study 61 identifies the figures of Revelation 12; this study reports the beast and the false prophet of Revelation 13 and later chapters, and does not take up the dragon, the woman, or the male child. The question this study alone answers: what does each passage say about a final ruler, an abomination, or an antichrist, and what does it leave unsaid?

S75.question: what is each person or group before the Cross said to have believed, and what had been said to them?
S75.distinction: Readers who already own Study 54 (Justification), Study 15 (Faith and Works in James and Paul), or Study 43 (The Gospel of the Grace of God) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 54 traces justification as a verdict and the means by which it is received; this study does not take up that verdict and reads only passages before the Cross. Study 15 reads James 2 and Romans 4 each within its own audience; this study does not compare the two writers. Study 43 reads Paul’s gospel as the gospel of the grace of God; this study does not restate it and reports what the earlier passages say was said to those who believed. The question this study alone answers: what is each person or group before the Cross said to have believed, and what had been said to them?

S76.question: what does Ephesians 6:10–20 say to do, with what, and against whom, and what does it leave unsaid?
S76.distinction: Readers who already own Study 30 (Seated With Christ in Heavenly Places), Study 57 (The Eternal Purpose of God), Study 48 (The Christian Household), or Study 22 (Prayer Under Grace) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 30 reads Ephesians 2:6 and the Body’s seated position; this study reports the shared word “heavenly places” and does not reopen that question. Study 57 reads Ephesians 3:10–11 on the Church’s witness before heavenly authorities; this study sets 3:10 beside 6:12 and does not read it on its own terms. Study 48 reads the household instruction of Ephesians 5:15–6:9; this study begins at 6:10 and does not take up that instruction. Study 22 distinguishes prayer instruction under grace from promises spoken elsewhere; this study reads only the prayer of 6:18–20 in its place in the passage. The question this study alone answers: what does Ephesians 6:10–20 say to do, with what, and against whom, and what does it leave unsaid?

S77.question: what does Romans 13:1–7 say the believer owes to governing authorities, and why, and what does it leave unsaid?
S77.distinction: Readers who already own Study 59 (The Law’s Jurisdiction and the Body of Christ), Study 76 (Strength to Stand), Study 48 (The Christian Household), Study 47 (Giving Under Grace), or Study 74 (The Man of Sin) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 59 reads the Law’s jurisdiction; this study reports Romans 13:8–10 as written and does not take that question up. Study 76 reads Ephesians 6:10–20; this study sets the word “powers” beside Ephesians 6:12 and does not read the armour. Study 48 reads the household instruction of Ephesians 5:15–6:9, and Study 47 reads giving under grace; this study reads only what is owed in Romans 13:6–7. Study 74 reads the final-ruler passages; this study leaves them there. The question this study alone answers: what does Romans 13:1–7 say the believer owes to governing authorities, and why, and what does it leave unsaid?

S78.question: what does each passage that names the Sabbath say, to whom does it speak, and what does it leave unsaid?
S78.distinction: Readers who already own Study 27 (Israel’s Seven Appointed Feasts), Study 39 (The Church’s Relationship to Israel’s Scriptures), Study 59 (The Law’s Jurisdiction and the Body of Christ), or Study 51 (Circumcision) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 27 reads the weekly Sabbath inside Leviticus 23; this study reads the Sabbath across every passage that names it. Study 39 uses the Sabbath as one sample of a method; this study takes up the passages themselves. Study 59 reads the Law’s jurisdiction, which this study does not take up. Study 51 reads circumcision as a covenant sign, and this study reads the Sabbath’s own sign passages. The question this study alone answers: what does each passage that names the Sabbath say, to whom does it speak, and what does it leave unsaid?

S79.question: what does each passage that names Sheol, Hades, Gehenna or the lake of fire say, to whom does it speak, and what does it leave unsaid?
S79.distinction: Readers who already own Study 31 (The Judgments of Scripture), Study 49 (The Resurrections of Scripture), Study 68 (The Book of Life), or Study 74 (The Man of Sin) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 31 classifies Scripture’s judgments by subject, time and outcome; this study reads the words for the place of the dead and the fire without classifying judgments. Study 49 traces the resurrections Scripture names; this study reports Revelation 20:13 as written and draws no resurrection teaching from it. Study 68 reads the passages about a book of names, including Revelation 20:11–15; this study reads only the clauses about Hades and the lake of fire. Study 74 reads the beast and the false prophet, which this study cites once as a cross-reference. The question this study alone answers: what does each passage that names Sheol, Hades, Gehenna or the lake of fire say, to whom does it speak, and what does it leave unsaid?

S80.question: what does each use of “the foundation of the world” say, with which governing word, and what does it leave unsaid?
S80.distinction: Readers who already own Study 68 (The Book of Life), Study 57 (The Eternal Purpose of God), Study 75 (Faith Before the Cross), Study 50 (Election), or Study 52 (Sonship and Adoption) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 68 reads the passages about a book of names, including Revelation 13:8 and 17:8 in that connection; this study reads the phrase “the foundation of the world” in every verse where it stands. Study 57 treats the eternal purpose and the Mystery; this study reports Ephesians 1:4 as written and leaves the Mystery question to it. Study 75 traces what earlier believers believed; this study reports 1 Peter 1:20 without adding to what they knew. Studies 50 and 52 treat choosing and sonship, which this study does not. The question this study alone answers: what does each use of “the foundation of the world” say, with which governing word, and what does it leave unsaid?

S81.question: what does each passage say about praying “in the Spirit,” “with the spirit” and “in an unknown tongue,” and where does the text itself tie them together or leave them apart?
S81.distinction: Readers who already own Study 22 (Prayer Under Grace), Study 25 (The Signs That Followed), Study 34 (Filled Again), Study 38 (Why Acts Is Not a Universal Experience Manual), Study 44 (Walking in the Spirit) or Study 76 (Strength to Stand) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 22 establishes prayer under grace; this study reads only the passages that speak of praying in or with the Spirit. Study 25 reads the signs that followed with the commission and audience in view, and Study 34 reads repeated filling in Acts; this study records what the three tongues accounts say and draws no rule of practice from them. Study 38 asks when an action narrated in Acts instructs the Body, which this study does not decide. Study 44 treats the Spirit’s ongoing ministry to the Body, and Study 76 treats the armour of God; this study reads only the verse about prayer that follows the armour. The question this study alone answers: what does each passage say about praying “in the Spirit,” “with the spirit” and “in an unknown tongue,” and where does the text itself tie them together or leave them apart?

S82.question: what did the law require of the one who redeems, and where does Scripture say each requirement was met?
S82.distinction: Readers who already own Study 53 (Redemption), Study 52 (Sonship and Adoption) or Study 71 (The Genealogies of Jesus) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 53 asks what is redeemed, at what price and for which company across Scripture; this study asks only what the law required of the person who redeems. Study 52 asks what legal standing Galatians 4:4–5 describes, which this study does not take up. Study 71 reads the two genealogies of Jesus, and this study reads Ruth for the steps of the redeemer and does not follow the line. The question this study alone answers: what did the law require of the one who redeems, and where does Scripture say each requirement was met?

S83.question: what does Paul say in 1 Corinthians 7, to whom, and on whose authority?
S83.distinction: Readers who already own Study 48 (The Christian Household), Study 1 (The Bride of Christ) or Study 36 (Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 48 reads the instruction to husbands and wives in Ephesians 5 and Colossians 3; Study 1 reads Paul’s marriage imagery; Study 36 reads other ground in the same letter and its neighbours. This study asks only what 1 Corinthians 7 says to the married, the unmarried and the widowed, and whose word each instruction is. The question this study alone answers: what does Paul say in 1 Corinthians 7, to whom, and on whose authority?

S84.question: what do Romans 8:17–39 and 2 Corinthians 4 say about suffering and glory, and who is “we” in each verse?
S84.distinction: Readers who already own Study 46 (Secure in Christ), Study 52 (Sonship and Adoption), Study 53 (Redemption) or Study 81 (Praying in the Spirit) will recognize adjoining ground. Study 46 reads Romans 8:28–39 for the security of the believer; Studies 52 and 53 read adoption and redemption; Study 81 reads Romans 8:26–27 on praying. This study asks only what these two chapters say of suffering and of glory, and who is speaking to whom. The question this study alone answers: what do Romans 8:17–39 and 2 Corinthians 4 say about suffering and glory, and who is “we” in each verse?

S85.question: what does Romans 1:18–3:20 charge, against whom, and where does it stop?
S85.distinction: Readers who already own Study 54 (Justification), Study 43 (The Gospel of the Grace of God), Study 59 (The Law’s Jurisdiction and the Body of Christ) or Study 35 (Who Is the Israel of God?) will recognize adjoining ground.
